Kentucky Straight Bourbon · James B. Beam Distilling Co.

Old Grand-Dad
114

A cheap-looking bottle with a serious old bourbon pedigree: high rye, 114 proof, unapologetically spicy, and still one of the clearest examples of how much character can live below the premium shelf.

Research current as of October 5, 2026 · Prices and product information reflect this period
114 proof / 57% ABV High-rye bourbon NAS · at least 4 years No secondary finish
The short version

A relic that survived long enough to become modern again

Old Grand-Dad 114 is not refined in the contemporary luxury-bourbon sense. It does not lead with age statements, bespoke finishing casks, elaborate bottle design, or scarcity theater. What it offers instead is a historically rooted high-rye Beam profile at 57% ABV: cinnamon, baking spice, caramel, dry oak, citrus peel, pepper and the nutty undertone that many drinkers associate with Beam whiskey.

The critical consensus is unusually coherent on its identity even when reviewers disagree on its quality. Breaking Bourbon’s 2025 review praises the expressive finish and extraordinary value while noting a somewhat tight, direct palate.4 Bourbon Culture likes the bold flavor but finds youthful grain, heat and rough edges.5 The Whiskey Shelf lands in a similar place from a different angle: dry, earthy, nutty and oaky, with enough ABV to give it energy but not enough sweetness or fruit development to make it feel fully mature.6 Bourbon historian Michael Veach, by contrast, described it as very spicy yet notably smooth for the proof, with citrus, caramel, tobacco, fruit, oak and pepper.7

House synthesis: OGD 114 is best understood as a very good, deliberately forceful bourbon sold at an unusually forgiving price—not a hidden 10-year-old masterpiece. Its strongest assets are identity, proof, spice and value. Its weaknesses are youth, dryness and a level of ethanol that can feel more assertive than 114 proof suggests.

Background

From Basil Hayden to the squat bottle

Old Grand-Dad is named for Meredith Basil Hayden Sr., the farmer-distiller whose grandson, Colonel R. B. Hayden, memorialized him in the brand. Beam’s current history places the first bottling of Old Grand-Dad in 1882 and emphasizes the family’s association with rye-forward whiskey.1

The modern brand’s path runs through the Wathen family, American Medicinal Spirits, National Distillers and ultimately Jim Beam. The ownership chronology is messy enough that reputable sources sometimes describe the Beam transaction as 1987 and sometimes 1988; the useful point for the drinker is that the Old Grand-Dad brand moved from National Distillers to Beam in the late 1980s, and production eventually shifted to Beam’s Kentucky facilities.8

The 114-proof expression is younger than the brand itself. Historical packaging and advertising show National Distillers selling Old Grand-Dad 114 by 1981, then touting it as “barrel proof” and a premium expression at a time when American whiskey above 100 proof was far less common than it is today.9 Bourbon Culture’s archival research likewise places the launch in the early 1980s and describes older 114 bottlings as a much more mature style than the current Beam version.10

1882

Old Grand-Dad is first bottled, named in honor of Basil Hayden Sr.1

Prohibition era

The brand survives through the medicinal-whiskey system under the corporate lineage that became National Distillers.4

1981

Contemporary National Distillers advertising documents the 114-proof “barrel proof” bottling in market.9

Late 1980s

Beam acquires National Distillers’ spirits holdings, including Old Grand-Dad, and later moves production to its own system.8

Today

The standard OGD 114 remains a batched, no-age-statement 114-proof whiskey; a separate 7-year single-barrel 114 expression joined the range in 2026.3

What is actually in the bottle?

High rye, new charred oak, and no finishing detour

The standard expression is Kentucky straight bourbon bottled at 114 proof (57% ABV) by James B. Beam Distilling Co. Beam’s current product page explicitly says the whiskey is cut to 114 proof, which matters: despite the historical use of “barrel proof” on older National Distillers bottles, the current standard OGD 114 should not be treated as an unproofed barrel-strength release.2

Widely reported mash bill

63% CORN
27% RYE
10% MALT

Multiple independent whiskey references report a mash bill of 63% corn, 27% rye and 10% malted barley, and the same proportions are used in current reporting on the new seven-year single-barrel release.46 Beam’s public OGD page describes the line as high rye but does not publish those percentages directly, so the exact split is best treated as strongly corroborated industry information rather than a currently posted producer specification.

Age and maturation

OGD 114 carries no age statement. Because domestic whiskey aged less than four years must carry an age statement under current federal labeling rules, the absence of one supports a minimum age of four years for the current whiskey.11 Reviewers often perceive it as roughly four-to-five-year-old whiskey, but the producer does not publish a specific age for the standard bottling. It matures as bourbon does: in new charred oak. No secondary cask finish is disclosed, and there is no reason to treat it as a finished bourbon.

Do not confuse the bottles: the familiar standard OGD 114 is a no-age-statement batched bourbon. The Old Grand-Dad 114 Single Barrel 7 Year, introduced in 2026, is a separate product with a seven-year age statement and single-barrel format.3

Critical synthesis

What reputable reviewers actually taste

The useful thing about reading across several reviews is not finding identical tasting notes; it is finding the flavors that recur despite different palates, bottles and review dates. OGD 114 has a remarkably stable critical fingerprint.

Nose

Caramel or brown sugar, cinnamon, dry oak, rye spice and citrus peel are the most repeatable notes. Peanut or generalized nuttiness appears frequently. Some reviewers also find apple, dark fruit, clove, leather or tobacco.

Palate

Cinnamon, baking spice and pepper lead. Sweetness tends toward caramel, brown sugar and vanilla rather than lush fruit. Dry oak, nutty Beam character, orange peel, tobacco and leather often follow. The proof can feel assertive.

Finish

Longer and more impressive than the mid-palate in several reviews: cinnamon, pepper, rye spice and charred oak linger, sometimes with molasses, toffee, tobacco or vanilla underneath.

High agreementCinnamon · baking spice · rye pepper · caramel · oak
FrequentOrange/citrus peel · peanut/nutty notes · vanilla · brown sugar · leather/tobacco
DisputedHow “hot” it drinks; whether the dryness reads as pleasantly old-school or simply young and underdeveloped.
Broad verdictGood-to-very-good whiskey, exceptional value, highly recognizable profile; not universally considered complex or polished.

Why the reviews diverge

The disagreement is less about what OGD 114 tastes like than about what each reviewer wants from bourbon. The Whiskey Shelf penalizes its dry, grainy, nutty profile for lacking richer sweetness and fruit.6 Bourbon Culture likewise hears the whiskey asking for more barrel time and prefers the balance of the 100-proof Bottled-in-Bond version.5 Breaking Bourbon’s more recent review is notably warmer, arguing that the high-rye spice profile remains distinctive and that the price has barely moved while the bourbon market around it has become much more expensive.4

Michael Veach’s 2017 tasting is useful as a check against the “only hot and young” reading. Veach—one of the better credentialed bourbon historians to publish tasting notes—found citrus, caramel, fruit, tobacco, dry oak and pepper, and judged it smooth for its proof.7 Taken together, the reviews suggest a whiskey that rewards drinkers who enjoy spice, structure and proof more than those searching for plush sweetness or deep aged-oak complexity.

Quality & value

The price is part of the argument

Breaking Bourbon listed a $35 MSRP for the standard bottle in 2025 and called it one of the strongest values in bourbon, noting that real-world shelf prices can be lower.4 That value context matters. A 114-proof bourbon with a distinct house profile is much easier to forgive for being direct, dry or slightly rough when it costs about the same as many entry-level 90-proof bottles.

This is not a “buy at any price” bottle. Its reputation was built precisely because it delivers a lot of bourbon for relatively little money. Once the price approaches premium single-barrel territory, the weaknesses called out by more critical reviewers become more important.

Comparable bottles

What competes with OGD 114—and what more money actually buys

There is no single perfect substitute for Old Grand-Dad 114 because its appeal sits at the intersection of several traits: high rye, high proof, a relatively young straight-bourbon profile, an old-school Beam nuttiness, and a price that remains firmly in everyday-whiskey territory. The most useful comparison is therefore not “what tastes exactly like it?” but which part of the proposition matters most to you?

Closest family resemblanceOld Grand-Dad Bottled-in-Bond. Same high-rye OGD identity at 100 proof and at least four years old, but generally calmer and more balanced. It is the cleanest way to ask whether you prefer the OGD recipe itself or specifically the extra force of 114.
Closest budget rivalWild Turkey 101. Another spicy, assertive Kentucky bourbon with a long-standing value reputation. It gives up 13 proof points but brings a published 6–8 year age range and usually reads more mature and integrated.
Closest proof rivalsWild Turkey Rare Breed and Old Forester 1920. Both sit around 115–117 proof and show what happens when similar intensity is paired with more expensive whiskey and, in Rare Breed’s case, explicitly older component stocks.
More age, same Beam familyKnob Creek 9. It is 100 proof and less rye-driven, but its nine-year age statement and Beam DNA make it a useful contrast: deeper oak, caramel and nuttiness, less raw spice, and more maturity for only a modest price increase.

So where does OGD 114 land on value?

At $32.95 in North Carolina, OGD 114 occupies an unusually favorable gap. It costs only $3 more than Old Forester 100, $5 more than Wild Turkey 101, and $8 more than OGD Bonded, yet jumps to 114 proof and retains a genuinely distinctive high-rye profile. That does not mean it is automatically better whiskey than those bottles. Wild Turkey 101 is older; Knob Creek 9 is much older; Four Roses Small Batch is more polished; Rare Breed and Old Forester 1920 are more complete high-proof sipping experiences. What OGD 114 does unusually well is deliver concentration and identity without charging premium-bourbon money.14

Value verdict: At roughly $30–$35, excellent / near category-leading. Around $40, still a good buy if you specifically want OGD’s high-rye 114-proof profile. Above about $45, the argument weakens quickly: Knob Creek 9 offers considerably more age for less, while the seven-year OGD 114 Single Barrel, Rare Breed and Old Forester 1920 begin to offer meaningful upgrades for the additional money.

In the glass

How to approach it

Beam recommends OGD 114 neat, over ice, or in full-flavored classic cocktails.2 Neat is the best way to understand why the bottle has a following, but a few minutes of air can help the nose separate from the alcohol. A small amount of water makes sense if the cinnamon and ethanol arrive before the caramel and citrus. In an Old Fashioned or Manhattan, the proof and rye content give it enough structure to remain recognizable after dilution and sugar.

Think of it less as a “smooth” bourbon and more as a bourbon with enough proof and rye to keep its shape.

Neat & a few drops of water

Start with a small neat pour to assess cinnamon, citrus and nutty concentration. Add water a few drops at a time when heat obscures detail; the proof provides room to adjust, while excessive dilution can expose the dry, youthful edge.

Rocks & an Old Fashioned

A large cube softens intensity gradually. In an Old Fashioned, begin with restrained sugar so concentrated bourbon remains visible; orange bitters or peel fit the documented citrus-spice profile.

Manhattan & Whiskey Sour

Expect a bourbon Manhattan with rye-like spice rather than the herbal character of a 95-percent-rye recipe. A Sour can use the proof and spice to stay present through citrus; sweetness and dilution need balancing.

Use with restraint

Heavy ice dilution and very sweet mixers can erase the distinction that makes this bottle useful. These cocktail recommendations are editorial inferences from documented proof and flavor, supplemented by Beam’s general neat, ice and classic-cocktail guidance.

Consensus scores

Where Old Grand-Dad 114 lands

These are representative editorial scores derived from the review consensus rather than a simple average of incompatible rating systems. The Bourbon Quality score is price-blind and asks how Old Grand-Dad 114 stands against other bourbons across the category—from everyday standards to premium, age-stated, single-barrel and limited releases. The Value score asks how much bourbon quality and character the bottle delivers at its current North Carolina ABC regular retail price of $32.95.

Bourbon Quality
6.2 / 10

Breaking Bourbon’s 2025 review favors texture and finish, while Bourbon Culture and the Whiskey Shelf report youthful grain, dryness and restricted fruit; Michael Veach supplies a stronger positive view. Concentration places it above ordinary Maker’s/Bulleit bourbon and well clear of Cleveland’s defects. More coherent bonded Old Grand-Dad has a small balance advantage; Knob Creek 9 and Michter’s ceiling supply maturity and evolution that proof alone cannot create.

Value at NC ABC Price
8.8 / 10

At $32.95, concentrated high-rye character remains excellent value approaching exceptional. The more restrained quality assessment trims 9.0 to 8.8; Turkey 101 at $27.95 and Knob Creek 9 at $39.95 frame the choice.

Where sources conflict, the article keeps the uncertainty visible instead of smoothing it away. Community reviews are useful as a secondary “consumer pulse,” but are not allowed to override better-sourced factual material.

Editorial verdict

Good bourbon, approaching very good. Exceptional value.

Best for drinkers who enjoy rye spice, proof, cinnamon, dry oak and a slightly rough-edged old-school profile. Less suited to those who prioritize soft sweetness, fruit, or polished age.
